turns.text: Hey Lloyd, I'm finally getting around to debugging the ACT training script. It's a pain.
That sounds tedious. What kind of errors are you seeing?
Just memory issues. I realized the architecture is still set up for the old sequential decoder where it outputs one step at a time, so the batch size has to be tiny.
Ah, that makes sense. Sequential decoding is indeed slower and heavier on memory. Did you try reducing the batch size further?
I did, but it's too slow now. I need to rethink the pipeline. Oh, and did you see the weather forecast for next week?
I haven't checked yet. Is it looking bad for your outdoor plans?
Yeah, rain every day. I'll probably just stay in and code. Anyway, back to the model, the step-by-step output is just not scalable for our dataset.
Understood. Maybe looking into parallel decoding techniques could help later, but for now, sticking with the current setup is safer.
Lloyd, good news. I refactored the ACT model. We switched the CVAE to output a 100-step trajectory in one shot. No more sequential generation!
That's a huge improvement for speed. How is the training stability now?

Much better. The one-shot approach handles the long horizon without the exposure bias issues we had before. By the way, my coffee machine broke again. Any recommendations for a repair shop near downtown?
Sorry to hear that. I can look up some highly-rated repair shops in the downtown area for you.
Please do. And regarding the code, I need to update the inference wrapper to match this new one-shot architecture.
Got it. Since it's one-shot now, the wrapper will be much simpler. Do you want me to draft a snippet?
Yes, please. Also, what's the best way to visualize these long trajectories? Matplotlib is too slow for 100 steps.
You might try Plotly for interactive visualization or just downsample the trajectory for quick checks.
